title: Assess the quality of apples for export

lessons.title: The apple export industry, its terms and its rules
lessons.html:
Background and structure of the industry

South Africa's apple industry is concentrated in the Western Cape, in areas such as the Elgin and Grabouw valley, the Ceres region, the Langkloof in the Eastern and Western Cape, and the Wolseley and Villiersdorp areas. Smaller plantings exist elsewhere. A large share of the crop is exported, mainly to Africa, the Far East, the Middle East, the UK and Europe, with the rest sold locally or processed into juice. The industry is represented by Hortgro, which covers deciduous fruit, and its research arm funds work on cultivars, storage and pests.

The value chain runs from producers to packhouses, cold stores, exporters or marketing agents, logistics companies and ports, and finally importers and retailers. Main cultivars include Golden Delicious, Granny Smith, Royal Gala and its strains, Fuji, Cripps Pink (sold as Pink Lady when it meets the brand requirements) and Topred and other red types.

Terminology you must use correctly

  • Class: the quality grade into which fruit is sorted, for example Class 1 for the main export markets.
  • Count / size: the number of fruit per carton or the diameter or mass range.
  • Ground colour and blush: the background colour of the skin, and the red overcolour on bicolour cultivars.
  • Defects: blemishes, bruises, hail marks, sunburn, russeting, limb rub, insect damage, decay.
  • Physiological disorders: problems not caused by pests or pathogens, such as bitter pit, superficial scald, watercore and internal browning.
  • Maturity indices: firmness, total soluble solids (TSS), starch breakdown and background colour.
  • Consignment / lot: the fruit presented together for inspection.

Legislative and logistical requirements

Apples for export are regulated under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990. The export standards and requirements specify classes, size, packing and marking. PPECB carries out the export inspection on behalf of the Department of Agriculture and is responsible for cold chain oversight under the PPECB Act 9 of 1983. Many markets also require a phytosanitary certificate, pest-free registered orchards and packhouses, and sometimes special protocols for pests such as fruit fly or codling moth.

To comply, the exporter must ensure the orchard (PUC) and packhouse (PHC) are registered for the market, packaging is correctly marked, residue limits of the market are respected and the consignment is presented properly to the inspector with the right documents.

lessons.title: Sampling and judging external and internal quality
lessons.html:
Drawing a representative sample

An inspector cannot open every carton, so the sample must represent the whole consignment. The rules are:

  • Use the sample size prescribed in the export standards for the number of cartons in the consignment.
  • Draw cartons at random from different pallets and from different positions in each pallet: top, middle and bottom, inside and outside.
  • Do not let the packhouse choose the cartons for you.
  • Record pallet numbers and carton positions so the result can be traced.

External quality

Open each sample carton and check every fruit against the class requirements:

  • Size and count: fruit within the declared size range and correct count or mass.
  • Colour: ground colour and percentage blush for the cultivar and class, using the colour charts that apply.
  • Shape: typical of the cultivar; misshapen fruit is limited by class.
  • Stem: present, not damaged; stem punctures allow rot.
  • Skin defects: bruising, hail damage, limb rub, russeting outside the stem cavity, sunburn, healed and unhealed wounds.
  • Pests and diseases: codling moth stings, scale insects, mealybug, black spot (scab) and any decay. Live pests of quarantine importance are serious.

Count defects per type and express them as a percentage of fruit inspected.

Internal quality

Cut a set number of fruit to check internal condition and maturity:

  • Firmness with a calibrated penetrometer on peeled sides of the fruit.
  • Total soluble solids with a refractometer, in degrees Brix.
  • Starch breakdown by staining a cut half with iodine solution and comparing the pattern with the starch chart for the cultivar.
  • Internal disorders: watercore, bitter pit under the skin, core flush, internal browning and mouldy core.

Compare each reading with the minimum or maximum in the export standard or client specification for that cultivar. Fruit that is too immature lacks flavour; fruit that is too mature may soften or develop disorders during storage.

lessons.title: Cold chain regimes and the inspection outcome
lessons.html:
Monitoring cold chain protocols for apples

Apples are climacteric. They keep ripening after harvest, and warm fruit softens quickly. Good practice is to cool fruit promptly after harvest, keep it at the storage temperature and humidity specified for the cultivar, and avoid temperature swings. Long-term storage often uses controlled atmosphere (CA) with low oxygen and higher carbon dioxide, and some packers use an ethylene-blocking treatment, but only according to the registered product label and the market's rules.

As an assessor you should check:

  • pulp temperatures of sample fruit with a calibrated probe before loading;
  • cold store and container temperature records and set points against the approved regime for the cultivar and market;
  • that data loggers or probes are placed correctly in the container;
  • that the container was pre-cooled and is in good condition with clean drains;
  • that pallets are stacked to allow air flow and are not exposed to heat on the dock.

Some cultivars are sensitive to low-temperature disorders, and others to superficial scald after storage, so follow the specific regime and do not simply set the coldest temperature possible.

Determining the outcome

After sampling, compare your defect percentages and internal readings with the tolerances for the declared class and market:

  1. If all results are within tolerance, the consignment is approved for the declared class and market.
  2. If results exceed tolerance for the class but meet a lower class, the consignment may be downgraded and must be remarked accordingly.
  3. If results fail, for example live quarantine pests, decay above tolerance or residue issues, the consignment is rejected for that market. It may be reworked and re-presented where allowed, or redirected.

Record your findings clearly on the inspection report: consignment details, sample size, defects found, internal readings, temperatures and the decision with reasons. A clear report protects both the exporter and the inspector if the decision is questioned.

Key points

  • Hortgro represents apple and other deciduous fruit growers.
  • Export apples are regulated under the Agricultural Product Standards Act, with PPECB doing inspections.
  • Samples must be random and drawn across pallets and positions.
  • Internal quality uses firmness, TSS and the iodine starch test.
  • The outcome is approve, downgrade or reject, always recorded with reasons.
